prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realization at the 10^-18 level of uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B012, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Nothing in the round-1 exchange weakened the scientific case, and several members sharpened it. The magic-wavelength lattice cancels the first-order light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is a distinct architecture from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). The realization half is documented in the lab book: roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, the gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, and clock-to-clock agreement across independent laboratories and fibre links. As an instrument builder I weigh the systematics campaign behind those numbers as much as the idea. The two-name credit has an invention half (Katori) and a realization half (Ye), and six of eight members now name the same pair. I would draft the citation to say what is new, namely the neutral-atom lattice with magic-wavelength cancellation, so it cannot be read as a prize for precision metrology in general or as excluding ion clocks.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is not the maturity or the lack of reproduction. It is the priority record for 2001 to 2005 and the breadth of credit. Lemonde and the SYRTE group worked in parallel on lattice and Hg proposals, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Boyd did decisive early demonstrations and evaluations, and ion clocks reach comparable accuracy. A two-name prize necessarily leaves these people out. I cannot verify the early record from the files available to me and am relying on recollection that the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstration trace to Katori and the 1e-18 and many-body results to Ye. A second weakness is that this is a measurement capability rather than a new state of matter, and the fundamental-physics payoff (varying constants, dark matter, a redefined second) is still prospective. I judge these to be reasons for careful citation wording and a documented priority check, not reasons to wait.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 but flags that his preference is a specialist's view, that the 1e-18 and redshift numbers carry the case, and that Lemonde-era priority should be checked; he also discloses his time in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I take the specialist caveat seriously, and I am glad that a Hall-lineage member disclosed it openly rather than leaving it to be inferred. As chair I do not think the lineage requires recusal: you report no joint work or financial interest with Katori or Ye, and your judgement is one of seven that agree for independent reasons. I suggest we record the disclosure in the minutes and in the final ballot notes, and that you remain in the vote. On your priority question I agree with the item you share with Mehlig and Lindroth: before a final ballot the committee should have the 2001 to 2005 record in front of it, with the Lemonde and Hg proposals and the first Sr lattice papers in date order. My view is that the concept and first demonstration belong to Katori's side and the performance frontier to Ye, and I would accept a change of names only if that record shows a shared origin of the magic-wavelength idea.

responses.point: Olsson says the 1e-18 and millimetre-redshift results are Ye's, so the citation should separate the concept (Katori) from the realization (Ye) rather than let performance records carry all the credit; she also suggested the committee might wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with your split and have changed my citation text to follow it: 'invention' stands on the magic-wavelength proposal and early strontium work, and 'realization at the 10^-18 level' stands on the JILA record. That wording also answers the narrow-citation concern you share with Mehlig, since it names the lattice architecture and not metrology in general. On waiting for the redefinition of the second I still disagree, and I note that you no longer argue for it. The redefinition is a standards-body decision that follows the science and is not part of the prize criterion. If we tied the award to it, we would hand our timetable to a body we do not control, and the demonstrated agreement between independent clocks is already the decisive evidence.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B036 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) as his lead, as a prediction followed by an unexpected experiment with independent reproduction, while naming B012 as his first alternative and calling it the more secure choice.
responses.response: Your answer to the maturity objection is fair: eight years of reproduction in many laboratories is not a thin record, and the flat-band prediction plus the 2018 observation is a real theory-experiment pair. I defer to you and Mehlig on condensed matter. My remaining difficulty is still the credit, not the physics. The committee has not verified the experimental record around Cao, Fatemi, Dean and Young, or the Bistritzer share, and you concede that these should be checked. Your own words, that B012 is the more secure choice if the committee wants settled understanding, describe the standard I am applying. I would like to hear whether you could support B012 this year without feeling that the moire result is being displaced, because I see B036 as a strong candidate for a later year, not a rejected one.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B029 (IceCube; Halzen, Karle, Spiering) as his lead, resting on the robust diffuse flux and the link to cosmic-ray origin, while saying he would not block B012 and accepting the collaboration-credit problem.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube first at the opening and I still regard the diffuse flux as a real discovery, so this is a disagreement about readiness of the credit and not about the science. You note that Pearce, Olsson and you proposed the same trio. That agreement shows how obvious the names look from outside, but it does not tell us who made the decisive construction and analysis contributions among hundreds, or how Baikal and AMANDA pioneers should be treated relative to Spiering. Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson each said they cannot defend the three without that evidence, and I cannot either. If you want B029 pressed in a later year, the committee needs a documented answer on credit, and a citation resting on the diffuse flux and not on TXS 0506+056 or NGC 1068. I note my mild proximity through Fermi-LAT and treat that as a reason for restraint when advocating it.

responses.point: Mehlig moved B012 above his own first choice B057 and asks that the citation state the neutral-atom lattice and its magic-wavelength cancellation, not precision metrology in general, and that the ion-clock community not read as excluded.
responses.response: I agree and have written the citation along those lines. The claim is about the lattice architecture: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms with many-atom interrogation. It says nothing about the optical-frequency comb or about single-ion clocks, which are acknowledged as earlier prizes and as parallel routes. Your decision to step back from B057 because of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang gap is, in my view, the right call under a three-person limit, and I would only keep it as a serious alternative if someone can show that the Kane-Mele theory and the Molenkamp experiment form a separable, defensible prize without the HgTe prediction. I do not think that has been shown.

uncertainties: The 2001 to 2005 priority record for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks (Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ye); I have not seen the documents and rely on recollection. A different conclusion there could change the names.

Whether the committee as a whole accepts the lattice architecture as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation wording adequately protects ion-clock and comb-based contributors.
Whether the unclaimed contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others will be seen as an unfairness that a two-name prize cannot cure.
Whether the IceCube credit question (collaboration of hundreds, Baikal and AMANDA predecessors) and the B036 experimental credit can be resolved for a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B012: my work is in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and involves no lattice-clock work, Katori, Ye or JILA. I note Kroll's lineage disclosure (Hall's laboratory) and Olsson's University of Tokyo fellowship as relevant to B012, and as chair I recommend they be recorded in the minutes without recusal. For B029 I keep my earlier disclosure of mild proximity through Fermi-LAT follow-up of TXS 0506+056 and a field close to neutrino astronomy, with no personal tie to the credited names.
